scope: Harden Delivery, Automations and Recovery SQLite operator snapshots against same-name parent ABA replacement and live-WAL private-copy drift.
implemented: All three operator snapshot paths reject canonical-path, symlink, hardlink, ownership, mode and parent-directory violations before opening SQLite.

Main database, WAL and SHM sidecars are pinned as owner-private 0600 regular files; the parent directory must be a real owner-only directory with mode 0500 or 0700 and no setuid, setgid or sticky bits.

A parent directory fd is held for the whole snapshot. Symlink resolution, lstat identity and opened-fd identity are compared; final cleanup forces parent replacement or disappearance to unsafe-parent even if a lower-level result was already available.
On Linux, a database without WAL is opened through file:///proc/self/fd/<fd>?mode=ro&immutable=1, binding SQLite to the pinned inode rather than a swappable pathname.

When a live WAL is present, only the pinned main database and WAL bytes are copied into a fresh 0700 mkdtemp directory. SHM is intentionally not copied; SQLite creates private coordination state for the replica.

WAL private copies are materialized and reopened through the pinned temporary directory fd under /proc/self/fd. Copy creation, digest verification, SQLite open and cleanup never resolve a swappable temporary pathname.

The implementation enumerates regular-file fds in the current process, excludes descriptors held by the snapshot itself, and proves SQLite holds the pinned source inode in non-WAL mode or the pinned replica inodes after WAL querying.

Source main/WAL/SHM identity, size, timestamps and digests are rechecked before open, after open, after querying and in finally. Source rollback journals, incomplete WAL/SHM pairs, sidecar appearance/disappearance and copy digest mismatch fail closed as drift or busy/corrupt classifications.

Temporary-copy cleanup unlinks fixed replica names through the pinned directory fd, verifies the directory is empty and still the same inode, and only then removes the private directory. Recovery also removes a freshly created private mkdtemp directory if pinning that directory fails.

The public operator entry points remain read-only: they do not create, migrate, checkpoint, chmod, pair an owner or write a Session lease while producing operator inventory or recovery bootstrap state.

sourceDatabaseParent.decision: The source database parent is opened only by the read-only operator. Owner-only 0500 is a valid least-privilege mode and must not be rejected merely because it is not exactly 0700; owner-only 0700 remains valid for profiles that create or remove files in that directory.
sourceDatabaseParent.rejectedModes: Any group or other permission, symlinked/non-directory identity, foreign ownership, or setuid, setgid or sticky special bit is unsafe-parent. A representative 04700 parent is rejected by all three products.

sourceStorageFiles.decision: Main SQLite databases and WAL/SHM sidecars must be regular owner-private files with exactly mode 0600.

walPrivateReplicaDirectory.decision: The private mkdtemp directory that creates, reopens and deletes WAL replicas must be exactly owner-only 0700. Unlike the read-only source parent, this directory requires write and execute permission for fixed replica filenames.

securityBoundaries: The snapshot does not defend against a malicious process running as the same UID or against root.
Storage and snapshot digests are consistency hashes only; they are not digital signatures and do not identify a trusted author.
There is no external monotonic or authenticity anchor in this batch.
The non-Linux fallback retains historical path-based behavior and does not have an equivalent Linux /proc/self/fd inode-binding proof.
The local tests do not prove a real production DSH installation, a real systemd deployment, or a real model workflow.
Operator snapshots are bounded and read-only; they do not establish full OS isolation for arbitrary worker code.
The evidence covers Linux x86_64 local behavior and repository engineering checks only.
